details:
LAST TRANSMISSION

Last Transmission: Forgotten Astral Artifacts by Humankind is an interactive web experience that tells the stories of NASA equipment left behind during space exploration.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Last Transmission allows users to explore space exploration artifacts through interactive pixel-art maps and storytelling. The experience features 12 artifacts organized into three acts: Moon, Mars, and Deep Space.

Users can choose between two exploration modes:

  • Guided Tour: A sequence of 12 stops presented in mission order. The map automatically focuses on each artifact and opens its corresponding story.
  • Free Explore: Users can independently explore the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space sections, select artifact locations, and discover their stories at their own pace.

Each artifact includes a creative first-person transmission, a factual historical explanation, and a link to a NASA source. This combination helps users understand what the equipment was, why it was sent, and what scientific knowledge or discoveries it helped make possible.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Educational value: Makes space exploration history easier to understand.
  • Interactive learning: Encourages users to discover information through exploration instead of simply reading a list of facts.
  • Scientific awareness: Highlights the contributions of equipment that often receives less attention than the missions themselves.
  • Reliable information: Connects creative storytelling with historical information and NASA references.
  • Engagement: Uses pixel-art visuals, interactive maps, and audio to create an enjoyable learning experience.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to make the history of space exploration more accessible and engaging, especially for younger audiences and casual space enthusiasts.

We want users to recognize that even when a mission ends, the equipment left behind can represent an important part of humanity's scientific achievements. By giving these artifacts a story and a place in the history of exploration, we hope to inspire curiosity about space, science, and future missions.

4. What tools and technologies did we use?

Our project was developed using:

  • React: To build the interactive user interface.
  • JavaScript: To implement application logic and interactions.
  • HTML and CSS: To structure and style the experience.
  • Vite: As the development and build tool.
  • JSON: To organize artifact information and story content.
  • GitHub Pages: To host and publish the website.
  • NASA and USGS resources: To obtain historical information and map imagery.
  • Audio resources: Music by Scott Buckley and sound effects by Hove Audio.

No specialized hardware or backend server was required. The project can be accessed through a modern web browser.

5. How is the project creative?

Our creative approach combines historical information with fictional first-person storytelling. Each artifact has its own “last transmission,” written as if the equipment could tell its story before being left behind.

We also designed a pixel-art visual identity, interactive maps, and a three-act structure to make the experience feel like an exploration journey. Instead of presenting abandoned equipment as forgotten objects, we give each one a narrative connection to the mission and science it supported.

6. What factors did our team consider?

During development, we considered several important factors:

  • Target audience: We designed the experience to be approachable for users around ages 9–13, as well as casual space enthusiasts.
  • Scientific accuracy: Historical information is supported by NASA or other relevant scientific sources.
  • Accessibility: We included accessible controls, visible focus indicators, readable text, keyboard interaction, and reduced-motion support.
  • User experience: We created two exploration modes so users can choose how they want to discover the artifacts.
  • Responsive design: We considered how the experience and story panels work on desktop and mobile screens.
  • Technical simplicity: We focused on creating an experience that works in a web browser without requiring special hardware or additional software.

Ultimately, Last Transmission aims to connect technology, science, and storytelling to remind people that the legacy of space exploration goes beyond the missions themselves.
